title: India TB Mortality Falls 38 Percent Since 2015, WHO Report Finds
excerpt: The WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2026, as summarised in a government release, puts India's TB death rate at 18 per lakh in 2025, down from 28 per lakh in 2015, with a 94% treatment success rate.
body:
• India recorded a 38% decline in tuberculosis mortality since 2015, compared with a global decline of 35%, according to the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 released on November 12, 2026.
  • In rate terms, the reports put India's TB mortality at 28 per lakh population in 2015 and 18 per lakh in 2025 — a fall of 10 deaths per lakh.
  • Treatment success among patients with drug-susceptible TB was 94%, the government release cited in the reports said.
  • Screening at scale is part of the story: more than 25 crore people were brought within TB screening, and 48.64 lakh cases were identified, including 14.97 lakh asymptomatic cases.

India has recorded a 38% reduction in tuberculosis (TB) mortality since 2015, compared to a global decline of 35%, according to the World Health Organization's Global Tuberculosis Report 2026, released on November 12, 2026.

The figures come from a government release summarising the WHO report, reported by ANI via Devdiscourse and in a fuller account by NewsAge. Attribution matters here: the 38% is a WHO report figure as presented in that release, not a count compiled by either news outlet.

Reading the 38% carefully

A percentage decline can mislead if it is read as a share of people. What the reports give, in absolute rate terms, is this: India's TB mortality rate is estimated to have fallen from 28 per lakh population in 2015 to 18 per lakh in 2025. One lakh is 100,000 people, so the rate fell by 10 deaths per 100,000 population over the decade.

That rate fall and the headline 38% are the figures as reported; this article does not recalculate WHO's underlying estimates. The comparison offered alongside them is global: a 35% decline worldwide over the same period since 2015, three percentage points smaller than India's.

The second headline figure is about treatment, not mortality. Among patients with drug-susceptible TB — the form that responds to standard drugs — the treatment success rate was 94%, the release said.

What the government credits for the fall

The release attributed the progress to intensified interventions under the National TB Elimination Programme, including proactive case finding, AI-enabled chest X-rays, rapid diagnostics, prompt treatment initiation and differentiated TB care. It also cited nutritional support through the Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana and the Ni-kshay Mitra initiative, and AI tools used to identify hotspots and predict cases at higher risk of adverse outcomes.

India met 96% of TB programme funding requirements through domestic resources, the release added — a funding detail that helps explain why the programme could sustain screening at the scale described below.

The screening numbers behind the claim

Between December 7, 2024 and November 8, 2026, the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan brought more than 25 crore individuals within the ambit of TB screening activities, conducted more than 11 crore chest X-rays and more than 3 crore nucleic acid amplification tests, the reports said.

Those activities identified 48.64 lakh new TB cases, including 14.97 lakh asymptomatic cases — people with no symptoms who would be unlikely to present at a clinic on their own. That asymptomatic figure is the most consequential in the release for transmission: finding and treating cases before symptoms drive people to seek care is how a programme cuts both deaths and onward spread.

NewsAge's account adds how the WHO estimates themselves were built. The report draws on the Registrar General of India's Sample Registration System, community-based verbal autopsy assessments and programme data from the Ni-kshay portal, and an Indian Council of Medical Research–National Institute for Research in Tuberculosis prevalence survey conducted in 2025, which India has shared with WHO ahead of an updated country profile.

What the figures do not say

The reports do not present the 38% decline as elimination achieved. The government's own framing, in the same release, is of sustained progress towards eliminating TB through early detection, timely treatment and patient-centred care, with further work planned on screening, diagnostics, preventive therapy and nutritional assistance.

For readers, the usable takeaway is narrower and firmer: on WHO figures as reported on November 12, deaths from TB in India are falling faster than the global average, the death rate is down from 28 to 18 per lakh since 2015, and almost all drug-susceptible patients treated — 94% — are completing treatment successfully.
